stem.en: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to 20 m/s in 8 s. You could find the distance it covers either from the area under its velocity-time graph, or from a kinematic equation. Which of these correctly gives that distance?

text.en: 80 m — from s = ut + ½at² with u = 0, a = 2.5 m/s², t = 8 s. That's also the triangular area ½ × 8 × 20 under the v-t graph — the two methods agree.

feedback.en: Correct, and notice why: the kinematic equation IS the v-t graph's area, just written algebraically. Getting the same number both ways is exactly the check this lesson set out to make.

text.en: 160 m — from s = ut + ½at², but leaving out the ½, which turns the triangle into a full rectangle.

feedback.en: This is the classic dropped-½ error. Without it, s = ut + ½at² silently becomes s = ut + at² — double the correct triangular area, since a rectangle (base × height) is exactly twice a triangle with the same base and height.

text.en: 20 m — using the final velocity value as if it were the distance.

feedback.en: 20 m/s is the graph's HEIGHT at t = 8 s (the velocity), not the area underneath it. Distance is accumulated over the whole 8 seconds, not read off a single instant.

explanation.en: This is the same idea from the very start of the lesson, seen from the other direction: s = ut + ½at² isn't a separate fact to memorise — it's the rectangle-plus-triangle area under a straight-line velocity-time graph, written as algebra. Whenever the two methods disagree, the arithmetic (not the physics) is where to look first.

hints.en: First find a from a = (v − u) ÷ t, then decide which method (graph area or equation) to use — or try both and compare.
s = ut + ½at² with u = 0: don't forget the ½. Compare your result to the triangle's area, ½ × base × height, using time as the base and final velocity as the height.
